Sixth Battle of Courland · 2nd Baltic Front · 10th Guards Army · 15th Guards Rifle Corps
РусEng

Ten days at Eglеs and Jāņaiši

A reconstruction of the fighting of 17–27 March 1945 south-west of Saldus, from the war diaries of the 96th and 98th Guards Rifle Regiments, the combat reports and orders of the 30th Guards Rifle Division, the operational report of the 15th Guards Rifle Corps, and the journal and findings of the staff of the Second Baltic Front — read against the ground on the Latvian 1:75,000 sheet the staff themselves were working from.

Where this is, and when

Heeresgruppe Kurland, Lage 01.03.1945 · the six Courland battles

Everything else in this file is drawn at 1:75,000 on three and a half kilometres of farmland. This is the frame around it: the whole pocket as the German army group itself mapped it seventeen days before the attack, and the place of the sixth battle in the eight months of the siege.

Lage 01.03.1945 · Heeresgruppe Kurland. The pocket entire: Windau on the north-west coast, Libau in the south-west, Goldingen in the middle, and the front line running as a heavy blue arc from the Gulf of Riga down to the Baltic. Two armies hold it — 16. Armee in the east, 18. Armee in the west — with XXXVIII. Panzerkorps holding the sector that matters here. Soviet formations are in red along the outside of the line. The red box and the ring are mine; everything else is the map.

The same sheet, at the Saldus sector. Frauenburg is the German name for Saldus and both are printed here, one over the other. Gruppe 290 stands to the west — the division whose records do not survive and which this file spends a section failing to read. The blue line below the town is the German main line as it stood on 1 March; the attack of 17 March came north across it. The cross-hair is where the 1st Battalion of the 96th went into the wood on 18 March, about 13 km west and 7 km south of Frauenburg. It was scaled off this sheet against the two printed place names, not georeferenced, and it is accurate to a kilometre or so — the precise ground is on the 1:75,000 sheet above.

The six Courland battles

Eight months, six battles

The German army group in Courland was cut off in October 1944 and never broke out. What followed was not a siege in the passive sense: the Soviet fronts attacked it six times, and the Germans numbered the attacks as they came. Between the numbered battles the line barely moved.

The sixth is the last. After 31 March there was no seventh — the front went over to the defensive on 30 March, and the group surrendered in place on 8 May 1945, a day after the general capitulation.

And nobody agrees when it started

The dates above are the German veterans' association count, which gives the sixth battle as 18–31 March. The army group's own daily situation maps do not agree with it, or with each other:

The sheet for 17 March is still headed 2. Phase – 5. Kurlandschlacht. The sheet for 18 March is headed 6. Kurlandschlacht and counts 17 March as its first day. And the closing sheets of the battle — 28 and 29 March, 1 and 2 April — carry an Angriffstag count that reckons back to 16 March.

Three German datings for the start of the same battle, one day apart, inside the same headquarters. It is a small thing, and it is a fair warning about every other date in the file.

What the 10th Guards Army was for

Within the sixth battle, the operation this file reconstructs had a stated objective, and it was not Saldus. The army commander gives it plainly: the crossings on the Ciecere north of Saldus — cutting the road and rail artery on which the whole German position rested.

The army attacked with the 42nd Army on a front of up to 50 km against five or six German divisions, and its own frontage was 40 km. The 1st Battalion of the 96th held roughly one kilometre of that. The wood it attacked at 10.00 on 18 March is not marked on either map above; at this scale it is smaller than the ink.

Situation map: Lage Ost — Heeresgruppe Kurland, Stand 01.03.1945, captured German records. Battle dates from the Kurland-Kessel veterans' association; the conflicting datings are from the army group's own daily Lagekarten of 17, 18, 28 and 29 March and 1 and 2 April 1945 (германские документы в русских архивах, фонд 500). Boxes, rings and the cross-hair added here.

The operation

17–24 March 1945 · Saldus axis

The idea

The Second Baltic Front's last offensive against the Courland bridgehead opened on 17 March on the Saldus axis with the 10th Guards and 42nd Armies. The directive came down on 12 March. Between them the two armies were to break the German defence on a front of up to 50 kilometres and destroy a grouping of five or six divisions; the 10th Guards Army's immediate task was the crossings on the river Ciecere north of Saldus. On the way lay the Saldus–Skrunda highway and railway, the artery holding the whole German position together.

The design rested on surprise. The artillery preparation was deliberately kept short — "calculated only for suppression, not for the destruction of the enemy fire system", in the army commander's words. Front headquarters pressed hard, fearing the thaw. And the jumping-off positions were never properly dug: the riflemen spent the night and half the following day in shallow scrapes cut in the snow.

It went in with real weight: 144 guns per kilometre of breakthrough frontage, 32 T-34s, 21 IS-122 heavy tanks, self-propelled artillery, and the 15th Air Army overhead. Four rifle divisions in the first echelon, two in the second, and a whole corps — the 19th Guards, with the 22nd and 65th Guards and the 256th Rifle Divisions — held back to exploit. The Front's own assessment afterwards was that the army began the operation "with clear provision and superiority in forces and means."

Thick fog put the attack back from 10.00 to 12.00 and finally to 14.00, decided by Marshal Govorov over the telephone on the reasoning that if Soviet aircraft could not fly, German ones could not either. It went in on the sector Balini, two kilometres west of Jaunmuiža, after ninety minutes of registration and thirty minutes of preparation — an hour and a half of ranging fire that told the defenders precisely where the blow was coming. To the north-east, the 42nd Army attacked at the same hour and cut the Dobele–Liepāja railway west of Blīdene station; by 19 March it had cut the Kaulaci–Saldus highway as well. That army lost 250 killed and 1,184 wounded on 18 March alone.

What happened

The first day worked. The 29th and 85th Guards Rifle Divisions broke the strongly fortified first defensive belt and drove four kilometres north through wooded, boggy ground in the first thaw. By nightfall the 85th held the line north-east of Ozoly to Jāņaiši, the 29th from Jāņaiši to Ķeniņdīķis, and the 30th Guards was closing on Baloži. Forward detachments went on to reach Dakas and Danči, two to three kilometres deeper. Then it came apart. Regiments chasing a withdrawing enemy split onto diverging axes through the forest, and the offensive dissolved into separate isolated battles before the second echelon arrived.

In darkness the 29th Guards drove a further six to eight kilometres, reaching Lazdukalni, Aizupji and Dzervītes. Then, overnight, several German infantry battalions with Nebelwerfer and — by the army commander's count — about sixty tanks came down from Saldus and took the forest between Jāņaiši and Dambiņi, closing the door behind them. Another thirty to forty tanks pinned the 85th Guards. The 30th Guards Rifle Division, brought up to exploit at the junction of the 85th and the 29th, was counterattacked in strength from the evening of 17 March, had its pre-battle formations broken up, and went into action in darkness in a completely unclear situation.

The Germans reacted within hours. On the first day radio intelligence already tracked 12. Panzer-Division shifting from north-east of Saldus to south-west of Saldus, and prisoners revealed 11. Infanterie-Division, a battalion of the 563rd and the 263rd fusilier battalion moving up from the Libau direction into the 10th Guards Army's sector. Between the 7th and 8th Guards Divisions the Germans held on to a salient one to two kilometres wide, so that the two divisions never got elbow contact and each had to turn a regiment inward to cover the gap.

The seal came down between eight and ten on the morning of 18 March. Tanks of 12. Panzer-Division with Panzergrenadier-Regiment 25 drove up the road to Jāņaiši and through the wood beyond it, and by ten o'clock held the southern forest edge from Jāņaiši to Purviņi. Panzergrenadier-Regiment 5, reinforced with thirty to forty tanks, went at the flank of the 85th Guards and held it there all day. Overnight on 17/18 March the breach had been closed in two places at once. In the 15th Guards Rifle Corps the 87th and 90th Guards Rifle Regiments were shut inside the forest north-east of Eglеs; in the neighbouring 7th Guards Rifle Corps the 19th and 30th Guards Rifle Regiments of the Panfilov Division were cut off the same way. The corps operations schema of 18–19 March shows both pockets on one sheet, with German arrows converging on the neck of each. On 18 March the corps second echelons — the 30th Guards Rifle Division here, the 47th Rifle Division in the neighbouring corps — were fed in piecemeal to reopen it, without artillery preparation. The 30th was ordered to attack in the junction between the 85th and 29th Guards — a seam, at Jāņaiši. Its main assault went in at 10.00 against a German line two hours old, and met the fire of armoured pillboxes. By nightfall the army had ceased to be an army and had become four isolated fights, and only then did the commander decide to stop and re-form a continuous front. By 21 March the attack was over; on 24 March the corps went over to active defence.

Why it failed — four verdicts

The division, 19 March: "The reasons for the regiment's failure are explained by its commitment to battle without appropriate artillery support and the necessary reconnaissance of the enemy."

The division again, 4 April, and this time it names a man by his post. The war diary of the 30th Guards Rifle Division for March 1945 closes with a formal вывод — a post-mortem — drafted by Teplyakov on 4 April, signed by the chief of staff Guards Lt.Col. Kolodyazhny, and approved in ink by the divisional commander Guards Maj-Gen Isaev on 5 April. It is the sharpest thing written about this action by anyone: "Командир 96 ГВ.СП. не уточнив огневых средств, не разведав что за противник находится перед ним, не подтянув приданную и полковую артиллерию, которая отстала в силу трудно проходимых дорог, при отсутствии мер обеспечения подразделений полка на марше, принял решение на немедленную атаку, что повлекло за собой лишние потери и неуспех полка в выполнении поставленной задачи." The commander of the 96th, having not established the enemy's fire positions, not reconnoitred what was in front of him, not brought up his attached and regimental artillery — which had fallen behind on impassable roads — and with no security measures for his sub-units on the march, decided to attack at once: which brought about needless losses and the regiment's failure. He is not named. The document is dated eleven days before the regiment's командир signs as Golobrodko rather than Cherkasov.

The corps, 12 April: the advance-guard regiment of the second-echelon division advanced slowly, its leading sub-units got drawn into an unnecessary battle, and its commander went off to Eglеs with part of his force and lost control of the regiment.

The Front: "The operation had no success and the assigned tasks were not fulfilled not because of stubborn enemy resistance, but exclusively through the fault of the poor leadership of the command and staff of the 10th Guards Army."

Before

the same ground, October 1944 – March 1945

Схема 16. Действия 10-й гвардейской армии в районе Салдуса. The published schema itself. Auce is bottom right, Saldus top left, and the whole advance runs east to west across the sheet. The key in the corner is the point of it: Положение войск на 31.10 · 12.11 · 7.12 · 25.12 — four dated front lines, and the distance between the first and the last is the width of this page. 30 гв.сд appears twice on it, once at the start line beside the 15th Guards Corps arrow and once up at the top by Saldus, which is the same division's two months in one picture. 290. Infanterie-Division is on it too, in two places — the formation that would be facing the 96th again in March, on ground a few kilometres away. And the farm marked Андулени at the bottom is the Anduļieni from which the 12th Panzer Division struck the flank of the 85th Guards on the night of 17 March. М. И. Казаков, «А мы с тобой, брат, из пехоты…», схема 16.

March 1945 was not the first time these divisions attacked this district. The 10th Guards Army had been grinding westward toward Saldus from the Auce direction since late October 1944. The published operations schema of that campaign carries four successive front lines — 31 October, 12 November, 7 December, 25 December — separated by a few kilometres each. Two months of fighting for something under thirty kilometres.

The same nine divisions in the same three corps: the 29th, 30th and 85th Guards in the 15th; the 22nd, 56th and 65th Guards in the 19th; the 7th, 8th and 119th Guards in the 7th. And several of the same German formations — 290. and 205. Infanterie-Divisions among them — appear on both schemas, four months apart.

Then Priekule in February, which also stopped. The army was pulled into Front reserve behind the 6th Guards at Vaiņode, and spent the interval on company and battalion exercises, some with live ammunition, working specifically on assault groups against permanent firing points. On 12 March the directive arrived to attack again, in the army commander's words, "roughly the same district where we had operated before".

That history is the reason for the single most important number in this reconstruction. A Guards rifle division at establishment held something over nine thousand men. On 17 March 1945 the 29th Guards mustered 4,337, the 30th 4,406, the 85th 4,253. Every division that attacked on 17 March was at under half strength before a shot was fired, and the 96th Guards Rifle Regiment went into the wood north of Eglеs with what five months of Courland had left of it.

Two bases. The ground is the Latvian 1:75,000 sheet with the reconstruction drawn on it in true coordinates. Staff schema is the operations map of the 7th and 15th Guards Rifle Corps for 18–19 March 1945, drawn for the General Staff (schema № 4 to map № 1355), shown at its own scale and without overlays. It is deliberately not georeferenced: it survives as a photograph of a folded sheet, and a least-squares fit against nine farms whose positions are known gives a residual of about 400 m — wider than the German position it depicts. Its value is what it shows, not where it puts it: the two encircled pockets, the German arrows converging on their necks, and the identification of 25 мп 12 тд north of Jāņaiši.

The base is the real sheet. Latvian 1:75,000 sheet 19-Saldus (Geod.-Top. daļa, 1929 edition), cropped to the battle area and georeferenced on its own graticule — the same fit that puts Saldus town within about 20 m of truth. Every overlay is drawn in latitude and longitude and converted straight into pixels of that scan. Solid rings are farms whose position is fixed on the sheet; dashed rings are farms named in the documents whose position is inferred from the bearings around them, because the 1929 sheet was surveyed in 1911 and does not carry farms created by the 1920s land reform. Unit blocks are placed against those anchors; dotted blocks are positions the documents name but this sheet does not reach.

Killed over wounded, from the divisional diary. Six thousand two hundred casualties in four days, in one army, for a gain of about a kilometre on this frontage. The heaviest day is 18 March — the day the 1st Battalion of the 96th was destroyed. On 20 March the army was officially not attacking and still lost 1,435 men, more than half the entire Front's total for the day.

Ammunition held, 17 March, in combat loads

Nature29 гв.сд30 гв.сд85 гв.сд

The 94th Guards Rifle Regiment reported its own holdings on 19 March: rifle rounds 1.11, submachine-gun 1.03, hand grenades 1.60, anti-tank grenades 2.79 — but 82 mm mortar 0.69, 120 mm 0.41, 45 mm 0.50 and 76 mm 0.25. The infantry had ammunition. The guns did not.

This is what a breakthrough was mounted on. The artillery order of 19 March allotted 0.15 of a combat load per gun of 76 mm and above for a forty-minute preparation against a trench system in a forest — while the 82 mm mortars, the one plentiful nature, were told to comb 1.5 km of woodland.

1st Battalion, 96th Guards Rifle Regiment

the unit, day by day

The battalion enters the offensive as the leading element of a relief attack and does not exist as a separate unit four days later. Guards Major Yermak lost a leg on this ground and was left where he fell, his orderly deserting with his belongings. The record does not name him. It does show that the morning of 18 March broke clear and hard-frozen at minus four to minus seven, that the whole army lost 2,302 men that day, and that wounded were still being carried in from the forward edge on 22, 23 and 24 March. It also shows that the merged battalion kept the 1st Battalion's number, and that by the end of the month it was being built back up a company at a time.

What the regiment was before it was the 96th. Bound into the same archival fond, in a дело whose catalogue entry gives no hint of it, is an order book of 1941. The 96th Guards Rifle Regiment was raised as the 837-й стрелковый полк of the 238-я стрелковая дивизия and carried that number until May 1942; in October 1941 it was on the Tula axis under полковник Швец. The men who died at Baloži were serving in a regiment that had been fighting for three and a half years by the morning it reached that farm. ЦАМО ф. 6391, оп. 165239с, д. 2 — catalogued without a date range; it is 1941, not 1945.

The regiment's own reports, and the sheet that did not survive

The 96th's daily combat reports for 1945 are one bound file — ЦАМО ф. 6391, оп. 165239с, д. 5, «Дело № 036, Боевые донесения 96 Гв.С.П.», 178 leaves, January to August. Every day of the war is in it, numbered in sequence: № 072 is 9 March, № 085 is 21 March, № 091 is 27 March.

The report for 18 March is № 081, timed 14.00, and it cannot be read. It is written in soft pencil on brown ruled ledger stock, and the digitisation has not held it. Six enhancement passes over the scan recovered the header, the opening words «1. Полк …», and on the facing page a single fragment — «…-60 [нрзб] пехоты)», consistent with the sixty infantry of the eleven o'clock counterattack but not proof of it. The information is almost certainly still on the paper; it is the scan that failed, and re-photographing that one sheet is the single most valuable thing left to do.

It has since been read again by eye, and more of it has come back. Set out below as far as it goes — nothing filled in by inference, every uncertainty left marked. [нрзб] = illegible; (?) = uncertain reading.

[ружейно-пулемётный?] и миномётн[ый](?) [огонь] по [боевым](?) порядкам(?) [нрзб]
Наблюдением(?) установлено(?) [нрзб]
[…] 60 пехоты и 6 танков […]

2. [нрзб] [действия артиллерии?] [нрзб]
[нрзб] сосредоточенного(?) огня(?) [нрзб]
[нрзб] но не(?) [нрзб]
В 12.45 отмечались [про]лёты(?) самолёт[ов](?) [нрзб]

[оборот] [нрзб] (в 50-60 мт от пехоты!) [нрзб]
Нач. штаба(?) [96 гв. сп](?) гв. [майор](?) [подпись] (Тарасов)
(ниже, тёмными чернилами, обведено:) иВ.[Л/Б]анцов(?)

Two numbered paragraphs, and they are two phases: point 1 is the order received and the regiment's execution of it, point 2 the artillery and the contact. That shape tells us what the lost lines carried — the route and the timings of the march in the first, the fire fight in the second.

Four things in it are new. Half past one in the morning, against the divisional diary's «в 1.00» written up three weeks later — the regiment's own same-day report is the better authority. Sixty infantry and six tanks, the strength of the counterattack, now first-hand rather than at second and third remove. «В 12.45 отмечались пролёты самолётов» — the only aircraft sighting in any document on this ground, and since the Germans had pulled every flying unit out of the Saldus–Skrunda area by January and disbanded Nachtschlachtgruppe 3 on 13 March, while the 15th Air Army had been reinforced by three whole corps out of the 3rd Air Army in February and early March, those aircraft were almost certainly Soviet. And on the reverse, in a report to the divisional chief of staff, carrying an exclamation mark that is not decoration: «(в 50-60 мт от пехоты!)» — fire falling fifty to sixty metres from his own infantry.

The header number is contested: read by eye it looks like № 6[3?]; the strokes under enhancement give a closed loop and an eight. The sequence in the same file — № 080 on 17 March, № 084 on the 20th, № 085 on the 21st — puts 18 March at 081–083, so it stands here as № 08[1?] with the query preserved. On method, for whoever tries next: background division and a mild gamma is as far as this scan goes, and unsharp masking makes it worse by embossing the paper grain. The pencil is below the scanner's threshold in places and no further processing will recover it.

Five men, counted

Combat report № 083, timed 18.20, carries the regiment's own loss line for the day of the attack:

"Потери за 2[0].3.45г. … убито 20, ранено 125, б/вести 5 чел."

Twenty killed, a hundred and twenty-five wounded, and five missing. This is the first sighting of the five in a primary document rather than in a divisional summary. The day-digit in the header is smudged and reads as 19 or 20; the three figures and the words «б/вести 5 чел.» are firm.

They are not named, and they will not be named here. The file runs to 260 scanned sheets across eight months and contains no nominal list of any kind — no именной список, no донесение о безвозвратных потерях. War diaries and combat reports at this level count men; they do not name them below officer rank. The five names exist only in the casualty returns, and those are in a different fond.

The merger is in the same file, in the regiment's own words, in combat report № 085 of 14.00 on 21 March: "Из оставшегося личного состава 1-го и 2-го сб сформирован один батальон." From the personnel remaining of the 1st and 2nd rifle battalions, one battalion is formed. Its reverse totals the whole action — "Потери, нанесённые противнику за период боёв с 18 по 21 марта 1945 г.: убито и ранено до 300 солдат и офицеров. Подбито 2 самоходных орудия и 1 танк." — and adds two words: "Пленных нет."

Every report in the March run is signed by the chief of staff, Guards Major Tarasov, over a second signature — the ПНШ-1, a guards senior lieutenant whose surname is legible as a shape but not as letters: an initial Г or Т, then five or six minims, ending -нов or -лов. He is the only other officer whose hand is on these documents throughout the fighting, and he is not yet identified.

The man

Yermak, Nikifor Lavrentyevich, as a young man. From the Doroga Pamyati collection of the Ministry of Defence portal.

The later portrait, in a modern colourisation of the original print. Field officer’s shoulder boards with two stripes; screw-back orders on the right breast, a ribbon bar and suspension awards on the left. The set is consistent with what the records give him — Red Star, Patriotic War 2nd class, Red Banner, and the medals — and if the Victory over Germany medal is among them the photograph is later than the summer of 1945. Which would make it a picture of him after the leg. A sharper scan of the shoulder board would settle major against lieutenant-colonel and date it either side of the promotion.

Born 20 April 1910 at Ivanovka, Ivanovsky district — the district has belonged in turn to the Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye and Kherson oblasts, and the records give all three. Into the army on 3 December 1932 through the Leninsky district office in Kiev. By March 1945 he had been a soldier for twelve years.

He had been written off once already. A loss return of the Western Front books him as missing in the Smolensk region between October and December 1941, as a major. He came back from that. Eglеs was the second time.

Awards

Order of the Red Star, 21 March 1940. Order of the Patriotic War 2nd class, North-Western Front, September 1943. Medal for Combat Merit, 3 November 1944. Order of the Red Banner, 25 December 1944, by order № 132/н of the Military Council of the 10th Guards Army, as a Guards major of the 96th. The recommendation sheet gives the deed as 23 December 1944 and names the unit as the 2nd Rifle Battalion: "In the battle of 23.12.44, at the breaking of an enemy defence with a strongly developed system of artillery, mortar and rifle and machine-gun fire — thanks to good training of the personnel, constant and faultless work of communications and established co-operation within the sub-units and with the attached means, of fire and of manoeuvre — the 2nd Rifle Battalion, after our artillery preparation, by a sudden concentration of the greater part of its fire means upon separate enemy groups, having overcome the wire obstacle and the minefields, took two German trenches, inflicting heavy losses on them in men and equipment. Under repeated counter-attacks the battalion firmly held the German pressure, and the enemy, leaving many corpses of his soldiers and officers on the field, withdrew to his start positions." The award followed two days after the action. The sheet also gives his entry into the Red Army as 1936, where his service card gives 3 December 1932; and it places him with the 2nd Battalion in December 1944, where the March 1945 documents have him commanding the 1st. Both discrepancies are recorded here unresolved — but see What his army commander wrote below, where the man who signed that award writes the same 2nd Battalion in print, and where the order is presented in person and photographed. Medal for Victory over Germany, 9 May 1945, awarded while he was in hospital.

On 6 April 1985 he was given the Order of the Patriotic War 1st class in the anniversary award. He was 74, and he was alive to receive it.

Service

He came to the war from the Defence Commissariat. A recommendation sheet made out while he was on the separate junior lieutenants' courses of the North-Western Front opens: "From the first days of the Patriotic War comrade Yermak works as an official of the People's Commissariat of Defence for the assignments of the Deputy People's Commissar. A number of tasks he carried out on the instructions and assignments of the Marshal of the Soviet Union comrade Timoshenko." Stalin took the People's Commissariat on 19 July 1941 and Timoshenko served as one of his deputies — so from the first weeks of the war this officer was carrying the Deputy Commissar's errands.

And in 1943 he was not in the line. A second sheet, made out under the place of service junior lieutenants' courses of the 2nd Baltic Front — the same establishment, renamed when the North-Western Front was disbanded that November to form the 2nd Baltic — assesses September 1943 and records that he had been working as commander of a company of cadets since that month — disciplined and demanding of himself and his subordinates, with enough military education and organisational ability to run the training process and hold discipline and order in the company, conscientious, systematically working on raising his own knowledge, good on the drill square, smart and soldierly in appearance, and devoted to the cause of the party of Lenin and Stalin. Not a word of combat in it. So the officer who took 1st Battalion into the wood north of Eglеs had come to a rifle battalion from running a cadet company, and his only combat decorations before Courland were the Red Star of March 1940 and the Red Banner of December 1944.

He served in the 98th Guards Rifle Regiment before the 96th, so he stayed inside the same division. Two officer service cards survive, and they close on different dates because they belong to different card series rather than because they disagree. One closes on 4 April 1945 with the rank of major — a fortnight after the wound, which is the personnel department closing its card once he had left the front for the rear hospital chain. The other runs to 30 October 1947 and gives his rank as lieutenant-colonel. A closed card does not acquire a new rank, so he was promoted after losing the leg and carried on the rolls for two and a half more years. What he did between leaving hospital in September 1945 and that discharge is not in any document here.

Out of the wood, and where he went

Three cards survive in the wound index of the military-medical archive, all of them giving his last unit as the 96th Guards Rifle Regiment of the 30th Guards, and all of them naming a different hospital.

ЭГ 1032 — Riga. The hospital stood there from 1 February to 1 June 1945. His card gives the reason for leaving only as evacuated to the rear, with no date. This is the first of the three and the one that put him on a train.
ЭГ 2637 — Rēzekne. There from October 1944 to mid-May 1945; he left on 22 May 1945, and by August the hospital itself had been shipped to Mongolia for the war against Japan.
ЭГ 3825 — Ivanovo. A fixed installation that stood in one place from August 1941 to December 1945. He left it on 13 September 1945.

Out of Courland to Riga, then 250 km east along the railway into Latgale, then deep into Russia — Ivanovo is north-east of Moscow, about 1,200 km from the wood he was hit in.

Hit on the morning of 18 March and not discharged from the last hospital until the middle of September: close to six months of treatment, which is what an amputation and the infection that follows days in the open actually cost.

Two of the three cards carry Ludza in the field the portal labels place of birth, while the third and his service record give Ivanovka. Ludza is in eastern Latvia, about 250 km behind this front and on the railway east. It is almost certainly a hospital location read off the card into the wrong field — and if so it is the first stop on the route out of Courland.

One earlier guess can now be dropped. It looked possible that a battalion commander left on the ground with his orderly gone would be booked among the five men the regiment reported missing on 18 March. He was not. He went into the medical chain as a wounded man, and the only time he was ever posted missing was in 1941.

In his own hand

N. L. Yermak's memoir, recovered 11 August 2026

Twenty-two handwritten sheets, written around 1975 and kept in the family. Most of it is not about the war: an open letter to Pravda in 1980, collectivisation work at Melitopol in 1930, a letter about a Kremlin concert in 1976. But on three sheets, inside a letter to All-Union Radio about the announcer Levitan, he sets down what happened to him — and he names the date, the army, the ground, the battalion, the regiment and the division.

The day

[нрзб] 18 марта 1945 года … 10-я Армия вела бои в Латвии, прорывала оборону в Курляндии. 1 батальон 96 гв. сп 30 гв. сд, в котором бою я был тяжело ранен. Передал свою [часть](?) начштабу Лебедеву(?) П. Н., а меня эвакуировали в медсанбат, где сделали первую помощь. Вечером(?) же дня эвакуировали в полевой госпиталь …

Eighteen months of archival work went into reconstructing that sentence. He had written it down.

Two things in it are new and are in no document. He handed over before he was carried out — to a chief of staff whose surname reads as Лебедев, a name that appears nowhere else in this reconstruction. And he was evacuated to the medical battalion the same day.

The forty-five days

Врачи … наложили гипс … и эвакуировали в Армейский полевой госпиталь. Врачи … медсестра … всё делали, чтобы спасти мне ногу, но угроза нависла над жизнью, когда началась … гангрена. Тогда началась борьба за жизнь. И вот почти через 45(?) дней мне ампутировали ногу. … переливали кровь непрерывно … и эта кровь спасла мне жизнь.

The wound index gave three hospitals and a discharge in the middle of September. This gives the shape of what happened inside them: the leg fought for, gangrene, the fight moving from the leg to the life, and the amputation about six weeks in — which puts it at the very end of April or the first days of May 1945.

Three o'clock in the morning

… 3 ч. ночи, слышу голос диктора Левитана. Он говорит: «Наши войска ворвались в Берлин и водрузили Знамя Победы над Рейхстагом!» От этого радостного сообщения где-то взялись у меня силы, я начал стучать рукой в стенку, пришла медсестра, и ей говорю: наши в Берлине … весь(?) госпиталь я поднял. … И никто не обиделся на меня за то, что нарушил их сон и покой.

Levitan announced the banner over the Reichstag on 2 May 1945. Forty-five days from 18 March is the end of April. So he lost the leg within days of that broadcast and heard it coming round in the post-operative ward, with the loudspeaker over the bed, and woke the hospital.

And the other wounded officer

Four sheets later he answers a letter from Guards Lieutenant Nikolai Krapiventsev, a platoon commander of his, about the fighting in the Baltic:

В лесу увидел раненого в обе ноги т. Крапивенцева, который сам засовывал в голенища сапог ветку, чтобы облегчить свои страдания. Я приказал его ординарцу и двум бойцам, чтобы помогли эвакуировать его для лечения в тыл.

He ordered an orderly and two men to carry a wounded officer out of a wood. Some months later he was the one in the wood. He does not draw the comparison, and it is not this reconstruction's place to draw it for him.

How much weight this carries. It is his own testimony and on some things nothing else can touch it — what he did before he was carried out, what the hospitals did, what he heard at three in the morning. But it was written about thirty years after the event, and this reconstruction has spent eighteen months preferring same-day paper to later recollection, including where a divisional diary written three weeks late disagreed with a regiment's own report. The same rule applies here. Where the memoir and a same-day document differ, both are set down and neither is averaged — which is exactly the treatment given to every other source in this file.

Sheets 15, 16, 17, 19–22 of «ЕРМАК НЛ сканирование 3113», 22 pages, family collection. Re-rendered at 300 dpi and background-corrected; uncertain readings marked (?), illegible stretches [нрзб], nothing filled in by inference. Sheets 3 and 4 remain untranscribed and sheet 4 is creased through the text.

What his army commander wrote

M. I. Kazakov, «А мы с тобой, брат, из пехоты…», Riga 1979, pp. 235–236 · received 19 August 2026

Army General Mikhail Ilyich Kazakov commanded the 10th Guards Army from 1943 to the end of the war. The 30th Guards Rifle Division was his. The order of 25 December 1944 that gave Yermak the Order of the Red Banner was his Military Council's order, № 132/н. In 1979, the last year of his own life, he published a book of memoirs in Riga — and on two of its pages he stopped the narrative of the campaign to write about one battalion commander. This is not a family paper and not an archive file. It is a printed book, by the man four command levels above him, published while he was alive to read it.

The page

I want to speak here of a man whose fate is inseparably bound up with the March fighting in Kurzeme. Somehow it happened that on the preceding pages of these recollections I did not mention him. And it must be done. If only because Nikifor Lavrentyevich Yermak — at that time a major, commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 96th Regiment of the 30th Guards Rifle Division — like many of our battalion commanders, fought not merely honestly and bravely but, if one may put it so, with relish. He was always a true workhorse, on whose shoulders lay his own military load and other people's too. That is probably because for Nikifor Lavrentyevich everything and anything was always «his business». In other words he was an active man, and though he did not like to push in «ahead of the father into hell», it worked out that he and his battalion were always the first into the military hell.

«Хочу здесь сказать о человеке, чья судьба неразрывно связана с мартовскими боями в Курземе… Никифор Лаврентьевич Ермак — в то время майор, командир 2-го батальона 96-го полка 30-й гвардейской стрелковой дивизии — как и многие наши комбаты, воевал не просто честно и мужественно, а, если так можно сказать, азартно… хотя не любил лезть „поперед батьки в пекло“, получалось же, что и он сам, и его батальон в военном пекле оказывались непременно первыми.»

«Первач»

First into the breakthrough, first to open fire because he was nearer the enemy, first into the towns and villages. The soldiers gave their battalion commander the apt nickname «Pervach» — and they pronounced the word with a mixture of affection and irony. Meaning that on the one hand he was strong and clean, and on the other devilishly insolent and bold.

The word is untranslatable in one go. Pervach is first-run spirit — the first and strongest of the distillate — and it also simply means the first one. Kazakov explains the joke himself: strong and clean, and dangerously so.

This is the only place in eighteen months of work where anyone records what his men called him.

Jaunserži, and the order

In the fighting near Saldus Nikifor Lavrentyevich was severely wounded, was treated in one of the Rēzekne hospitals, lost his leg. And some months before that I had the chance to watch his battalion's attack from my own observation post. This was at the farmstead of Jaunserži — some fifteen kilometres from Saldus. The attack was so swift, so strong, that the fascists had no time to take either the mortar battery or the two tractors with guns off the farm. After the attack I was told that the battalion commander in that action also saved the life of a platoon commander, Lieutenant Krapiventsov, severely wounded in the legs.

Every checkable thing in that paragraph checks. The wound index gives ЭГ 2637 at Rēzekne. The leg is in the record. And the Krapiventsev rescue is the episode Yermak himself set down thirty years later in a letter to All-Union Radio — where he gives no place at all. Kazakov gives the place.

The photograph

It gave me enormous pleasure that day to present Major Yermak with the Order of the Red Banner. He was photographed at the same time beside the unfurled Guards banner of his regiment.

And the photograph is in the family's box. Winter fur cap; field officer's shoulder boards with two stripes; a cluster of screw-back orders on the right breast and a suspension award on the left. Behind him the banner cord and tassel, and the lettering «…ЕМЕЦКИМ ЗАХВАТЧИКАМ» — the reverse face of a Soviet Guards colour, Death to the German invaders. The obverse inscription shows through the cloth mirrored. Nobody in the family knew what the day was.

And it was published at the time

Pasted into the album on top of a newspaper of about 1980, so the cutting itself is undated — but it is the same negative, cropped tighter and screened for print.

«Герои боёв за Прибалтику»

In the photograph: (right) N. L. Yermak. In battle the men of his sub-unit show high examples of soldierly skill and Guards valour. For an excellently conducted action officer Yermak has been awarded the Order of the Red Banner. (Left) section commander Guards Senior Sergeant Yershov. Immediately after the action he received the Order of Glory 3rd class. Photograph by F. Samusev.

So the banner picture was not a private keepsake. It was a press photograph, taken for the army paper on the day of the presentation, and the caption says in as many words what the order was for.

A new name, and a cheap one to chase. Guards Senior Sergeant Yershov, section commander, Order of Glory 3rd class awarded immediately after the action of 23 December 1944 — that is a single query in the award database, and it would give the second man in the frame.

The battalion number, again

Kazakov writes 2nd Battalion. So does the recommendation sheet of December 1944. The regiment's own reports of March 1945, the divisional diary, and Yermak's own memoir all write 1st Battalion.

This is not a third vote. Kazakov signed the December award. Preparing a book thirty-five years later, an army commander writing about a major he met once will have gone back to the file he signed — and the file says 2nd Battalion. The most economical reading is that there is one December document behind both, and that he commanded the 2nd Battalion in December 1944 and the 1st in March 1945.

That is a reading, not a finding. Both are left standing, as everywhere else in this file.

What it does not say

Kazakov gives 18 March 1945 one clause — severely wounded, Rēzekne, lost his leg. He does not say where on the ground, or who carried him, or how long he lay there. The family's account of an orderly who disappeared is neither confirmed nor contradicted here.

He also puts the wound "in the fighting near Saldus" without a date, and he is writing in 1979 about a man he could have telephoned. The reconstruction's rule holds: this is a memoir, and where it meets same-day paper the paper is preferred. It happens that on every point where they can be compared, they agree.

What it changes. Before today the only voices for this man were forms — a service card, an award file, a casualty return — and his own hand. Now there is a third: someone who watched him work and thought him worth two pages of a book about an army.

Казаков М. И. «А мы с тобой, брат, из пехоты…» (Воспоминания командарма). Вступление и литературная запись Г. Курпнека. Рига: Лиесма, 1979, с. 235–236. Photographed from the family's copy, 19 August 2026. The banner photograph and the newspaper cutting are from the family collection, Old_photos. The cutting's title and date of issue are not preserved; the photographer is given on the cutting as Ф. Самусев.

The operation from the army commander's chair

M. I. Kazakov, same book, pp. 226–239 · 12–30 March 1945

Nine further pages of the same memoir arrived on 19 August 2026, and they are not about one man. They are the 10th Guards Army's own commander narrating the whole operation — the directive that started it, the day it went wrong, the morning the Front commander walked into his command post, and the order that turned the attack into a rescue. The set is now complete: pages 226 to 239, the last four of them arriving after the first nine.

The plan, from 12 March

After Priekule the army went into Front reserve behind the 6th Guards, at Vaiņode, and trained assault groups against permanent firing points. Govorov's directive to prepare a new offensive came on 12 March — six days before.

The attached 83rd and 110th Corps widened the army's frontage to 40 km in exchange for five thin divisions, which Kazakov says plainly they were not pleased about. The operation was a Front operation with the 42nd Army, breaking a 50 km front against five or six German divisions. The army's immediate objective was the crossings on the Ciecere north of Saldus.

At the last moment Govorov added the 47th and 256th Rifle Divisions and took the 119th Guards into his own reserve. The artillery preparation was to be short, and for suppression only, not destruction.

17 March, and the crack

And that attack — 17 March — was one of a kind.

He watched it from his own observation post: the 29th Division's frontage and the right flank of the 7th. It began well. Then the reports turned. By dusk the neighbouring division had made 1 to 1.5 km, to Kauņi, and another was not moving at all. The 42nd Army lost its pace.

The tactical defence was broken in daylight on the Kauņi–Dangas sector. But at the junction of the 7th and 8th Guards Divisions the positions of one German infantry battalion were left untouched, and that is the whole story of the following week.

The commander of the 7th Guards Corps did not at once grasp the danger and, in substance, took no radical measures until the evening of 18 March. Nor did the army staff see anything threatening in the salient that had formed. — An army commander writing that about his own headquarters, in print, in 1979.

The night, and the sixty tanks

In the night the Germans counter-attacked out of Saldus against the right flank of the 15th Guards Corps and got into the rear of the 29th Division, which was still going north as though nothing had happened. Several infantry battalions, six-barrelled mortars and about sixty tanks cut it off.

Infantry with 30–40 tanks pinned the 85th; then the 5th Motorized Regiment and the 12th Panzer Division, with 30–40 tanks and assault guns, struck its flank from south of Anduļieni. The 253rd Guards Rifle Regiment was faced east from Skuinieki to Zariņi. The 251st, coming up in second echelon under Lt.Col. S. A. Grishchenko, fought at Zariņi and with three IS tanks and an anti-tank battalion burned twelve German tanks, then came into the front line east of Jāņaiši.

Jāņaiši. The same farm from which, at 11.00 on 18 March, sixty infantry and six tanks came out at the 1st Battalion of the 96th.

Morning, 18 March

By that morning the main body of the 8th Guards was cut off, the army was strung across a wide front in half a dozen separate pockets, and the troops had used no more than 0.8 of a basic load. Kazakov was preparing to report that the operation could still succeed.

On the morning of 18 March he came to the command post of the 10th Guards Army himself. This was unusual in his practice… his sudden appearance at the army command post put me on my guard at once.

Govorov looked at the map on the table, and then —

Leonid Aleksandrovich asked me to explain what had prevented the 30th Guards Division from coming up onto the line of the 29th, and why the salient at the junction of the 7th and 8th had not been eliminated in time.

That question is about this battalion. The 30th Guards is Yermak's division. On the morning of 18 March 1945, while the 96th was moving up through the dark towards the wood north of Eglеs, the Marshal commanding the Leningrad Front stood over a map at army headquarters and asked why that division had not come up. The assault at 10.00 is the answer being given to him. Until today this reconstruction could say only that the 30th was the corps second echelon, committed on 18 March. It can now say who wanted it forward, and at what hour he asked.

«Нельзя так наступать»

You cannot attack like this. You should have moved the battle formations of the corps and divisions forward evenly from the very beginning. Apart from what has already been issued, the army will get no ammunition. There is none in the Front's depots. So you are now to see to bringing the twenty-ninth and the eighth out of encirclement. Only after that can we think about continuing the attack…

Then he left, without saying how it was to be done. The chief of staff, Maj.Gen. N. P. Sidelnikov, passed it to the 15th and 7th Corps. The commander of the 29th was astonished — his men were under no direct pressure at all. He got the division out along forest tracks on the night of 18/19 March; the regiment covering the withdrawal stayed inside a further night and walked out by the same tracks.

The other pocket, to 28 March

Two regiments of the 8th Guards, the 19th and 30th, were pulled back in order. The 23rd, with the 26th of the 7th Guards, cut off the salient at Dzeni–Lapas. But the neck was not closed: the forest roads were swept by fire, ammunition and food went in on men's backs at night, and most men carried two submachine guns, one of them German.

25 March: the crisis. Three German divisions closed on the Panfilov men and attacked from several directions for two days, with loudspeakers telling them to surrender.

The relief was worked out on the ground by Kazakov and Maj.Gen. A. D. Kuleshov of the 7th Guards Corps; the battalions came from Gen. A. T. Stuchenko's 19th Corps — the 67th Regiment of the 22nd Guards Division, reinforced with a separate company. At 09.10 on 28 March, after an intense bombardment, it attacked; the 8th Guards attacked to meet it; and between 10.00 and 16.00 all the wounded were brought out.

The 67th of the 22nd Guards is V. V. Koreshev's regiment — the man whose notes, «Последний бой», Kazakov quotes immediately after the passage about Yermak.

Two men, and an archive reference

Lt.Col. Ivan Leontyevich Shapshaev, commanding the 19th Rifle Regiment, made Hero of the Soviet Union: a shell splinter took off his right arm and he stayed with the regiment and went on commanding it. Kazakov cites ЦАМО ф. 33, оп. 793756, д. 54, лл. 159–161.

Junior Sergeant Nikolai Nikolayevich Kislov, reconnaissance company of the 13th Engineer-Sapper Brigade, Order of Glory 1st class: in the German rear south-west of Saldus from 17 to 21 March, reporting fortifications and movement by radio, found twice, severely wounded, and finished the task. Cited from the Order of Glory card index, inv. № 928.

Kazakov also cites «Незабываемые дороги: боевой путь 10-й гвардейской армии» (Moscow, Voenizdat, 1974, 288 pp.) at pp. 249–252 for the night action of the 251st and 253rd at Zariņi and Jāņaiši. That is the published unit history of the army this battalion belonged to, and those four pages cover the night of 17/18 March on the ground immediately to the right of it. It is the nearest unread printed source to the night this reconstruction is built on, it is not in this project's holdings, and it is an ordinary second-hand purchase rather than an archive request.

And one claim to check

Breaking out of the ring, the Panfilov men did not lose a single man.

That should be tested against the loss returns of the 8th Guards for 26–28 March, and it is written down here so that it can be. It is the kind of sentence a memoir published in 1979 was expected to contain, and this file does not pass those on unmarked.

Two other things in these pages are internally inconsistent and are recorded as printed rather than tidied: the same divisional number, 198th, is given to two different formations in consecutive sentences on p. 229, and the first-echelon corps on p. 227 read as «15-й и 17-й» where the 10th Guards Army had no 17th Corps.

The weather. Govorov pressed them because the thaw was coming: fog in the mornings, snow melting by day, roads going soft, artillery — «our main technical strength» — losing its footing, and the weather unfavourable to aviation as well. That last clause belongs beside the aircraft at 12.45.

17 March, hour by hour

Page 228 arrived last and it rewrites the first day. The troops took up their start positions in the night of 17 March, and Kazakov admits at once what was wrong with them:

We had not managed to prepare the start line properly in engineering terms. The riflemen were in shallow scrapes dug in the melting snow, and of course they could not shelter reliably from the enemy's fire.

The morning came in foggy and raw, with no visibility at all. The attack was put back to 10.00, then to 12.00. By then the fog had lifted and wet snow had started. Nothing could be made out ahead. Air support, he writes, was not worth thinking about.

The telephone call at one o'clock

— Well, how is the mood?
— Not good, I answer. The soldiers have already been lying in the snow for hours. They cannot be kept like that any longer. It has to be decided: attack now, or pull the troops back to get warm.
— And how do you view it if you have to attack without support from the air?
— If our aircraft cannot operate, then plainly the enemy's aviation will be in the same position. Consequently the balance of forces does not change.
— Well then, you will have to carry out the task in a duel of ground forces.

And Govorov ordered the attack to begin at 14.00.

Four hours of light — and tomorrow

The postponements cost the whole shape of the day. Kazakov had to reckon that on the first day of the offensive his troops would have no more than four hours of daylight, and he wanted the first-echelon divisions to get through the tactical depth in that time. They were less well prepared for night work. So:

It was better to rest during the night, and on the following day to resume the fighting with the second echelons of the corps taking part.

That is the 30th Guards. Its commitment on 18 March was not improvised in response to a crisis — it was in the plan before the first shot on the 17th. What Govorov's question the next morning added was urgency.

Page 228 also names the army's own second echelon: the 19th Guards Rifle Corps — whose commander, Stuchenko, later gave up the 67th Regiment for the relief.

And the sky, on the day before

On 17 March there was no flying at all, by the army commander's own account, and the reasoning he gave the Front commander is worth having in full: if ours cannot fly, neither can theirs, so the balance does not change.

That is the day before the aircraft at 12.45. It does not decide whose they were — the weather on the 18th was a different day's weather — but it is the closest first-hand statement about air activity over this ground that this reconstruction has, and it says neither side was flying twenty-four hours earlier.

Koreshev, from inside the relief

Pages 237–239 are the notes of Guards Senior Lieutenant V. V. Koreshev, a rifle company commander of the 67th Regiment, 22nd Guards Division — the regiment that broke through to the Panfilov men on 28 March. Kazakov prints them "almost word for word".

His company was replacements: born 1926 and 1927, never in action, mostly from Leningrad and its province. Many of them had relatives who starved to death during the blockade.

They were watching a film in a plank cinema in the pine wood — «В 6 часов вечера после войны», At six in the evening after the war — when the alarm went. They never saw the end of it. On the road the soldiers joked: never mind, we'll finish it at six in the evening after the war.

The ground they had to attack over

Past the farm of Pampāļi, platoons 50 m apart because German shells were coming down methodically either side of the road. Eight hundred metres from the front line the army commander's car overtook them, and the general with the pleasant moustache leaned out to ask why a company was strung out like a division.

The start position was mossy bog, ringed with stripped and splintered aspens. You cannot dig in: put a spade in and the hole fills at once with spring water. And you cannot not dig in: one stray shell can destroy a whole platoon. He had them build breastworks of turf instead.

His verdict on why every earlier attempt to reach the pocket had failed: a reinforced defence, and wood and bog — ground where tanks cannot be committed and artillery cannot suppress the firing points.

The ultimatum, and the ten-minute deception

The Germans put the surrender demand to the encircled men over loudspeakers more than once — their lives guaranteed, or else they would be ground into the mud. The deadline they set was 10.00 on 28 March 1945.

Early that morning the company commanders were called to the regimental command post, and the attack order was given by the army commander himself.

Comrades, you have all evidently heard the Germans' ultimatum to the encircled men… We must break through at all costs and get our comrades out.

Instead of the hour-long preparation the enemy would be expecting, they fired a five-to-ten-minute massed strike from every gun, mortar and Katyusha, then lifted into the depth and sent the assault companies in behind it.

One round, kept back

And here is the first Panfilov man on our sector, the first out of the encirclement. Tears of joy in his eyes, filthy all over, bearded, shouting «Brothers!! Brothers! Our own!» — he threw himself at us. «Thank you! One round left… I was keeping it for myself. Thank you! You got us out!»

Then in twos and threes the rest, and they were sent straight back through.

Koreshev did not finish the day. Three kilometres on, halting his company at a wood edge with a farm 500 m ahead and no movement in it, he raised his hand to signal the advance and saw the muzzle flash from a barn. Ferdinands. The third shell blinded him; splinters went into the tree; his left arm, thrown across his heart, was pierced above and below the elbow. He had the two worst-wounded men carried out on ground-sheets and walked back with the rest.

And then it stopped. On 30 March the 2nd Baltic Front went over to the defensive on the ground it had taken. The 10th Guards Army held a front of over 40 km, from Deriņi south of Lake Ciecere to Papsas on the Venta, and most of its formations went to the rear to be brought back up to strength. Kazakov's own verdict on the whole plan is that it could not have worked: there were never enough men or enough equipment, and — paradoxical as it may seem — the further the Germans were pushed back into the peninsula, the better, not the worse, their capacity to defend it became.

A correction the photographs forced, 19 August 2026. Kazakov quotations were already in the day-by-day cards before these pages arrived, taken from a text found online rather than from the book. Set against the photographs, two of them had been paraphrased inside quotation marks, and one carried an hour — 11.00 on 18 March — that the printed page does not contain; the page says only «утром». An inference had been built on that hour. Both quotations are now the page text, the hour is gone, and the inference with it. Four further Kazakov cards quote passages that are not on pages 226–239 at all; they may come from a fuller edition or from his other memoir, and until that is settled they are marked «не найдено на с. 226–239» rather than left to look verified.

Казаков М. И. «А мы с тобой, брат, из пехоты…» (Воспоминания командарма). Рига: Лиесма, 1979, с. 226–239. Photographed from the family's copy, 19 August 2026; the set is complete. Full Russian transcription in 15_memuary/KAZAKOV_226-239.md.

The film

18 March 1945 · one battalion · 3.8 × 3.2 km · 01.00 to 20.00

Everything above is the divisional and corps view. This is the same day at the scale the battalion actually fought it — a frame less than four kilometres across, running in real order from the march in darkness to the burial parties. It draws only what a document places. Where a counter is dashed, its position is inferred from the axis and not written down anywhere; where the frame greys over, no document places anyone at all; and where two documents disagree, both are drawn and neither is averaged.

night
00:55Moscow time
Soviet German position inferred, not documented the division's clock, where it differs fire on its own infantry

Base geometry from the Latvian 1:75,000 sheet 19-Saldus, the divisional overlay for 18.03.45 and the artillery staff's plot of the German positions. Between two documented fixes a counter moves in a straight line at constant speed: that is drawing, not evidence. Light and darkness are computed for 56°36′N 22°17′E on 18 March 1945 and shown on Moscow time, which is what the Soviet staffs kept — sunrise 07:38, sunset 19:42. If any of these timings is in fact Berlin time, subtract two hours and the march begins deeper in the night than it already does.

What this frame cannot show

The two regiments it was all for are four kilometres north of the top edge. The decisions that governed the day were taken in Riga and at corps. And on the German side there is no counterpart to any of this: the Bundesarchiv holding for the division the Soviet gunners identified opposite, RH 26-290, contains nothing at all from 1945. Everything blue on this map is drawn from what Soviet observers reported seeing.

The men

96th Guards Rifle Regiment, 18–19 March 1945

For eighteen months this reconstruction could name officers and count everyone else. The reason turns out to be mechanical: casualty records index men by field post number, not by unit name, and the 96th was полевая почта 36586. Searched that way, the regiment's dead have names.

Almost every man killed on 18 March is recorded at the same place — х. Баложи, южнее, 200 м, two hundred metres south of Baloži. The officers and most of the 19 March dead lie two hundred metres north of Āres. Those who died of wounds went through the 29th medical battalion and were buried four hundred metres west of Budenieki, on a rise, in a common cemetery. All were later reburied at Mastīņi in Kursīši parish.

One name will stop you, and it should be said plainly rather than left to be stumbled over. Ермак Иван Стефанович — junior sergeant, from Klochkovo in Chernihiv oblast, indexed twice with his patronymic and birth year garbled between the entries — died of wounds on 19 March in the 29th medical battalion and lies in grave № 2. He is no relation to Guards Major Ермак Никифор Лаврентьевич, born 1910 at Ivanovka, who commanded the 1st Battalion and lived. But a man of that name died in the same medical battalion that had taken the battalion commander's leg the day before.

These are index entries — донесения о безвозвратных потерях, картотеки, списки захоронений and ВПП records — not yet checked against the signed sheets. Two captains, two lieutenants and a junior lieutenant of one regiment in two days; a guards lieutenant among the missing.

Память народа, картотеки и донесения о потерях; поиск по последнему месту службы «96 гв. сп» и по полевой почте 36586, выбытие 18–19.03.1945 — 57 документов

Inside the corridor

87th and 90th Guards Rifle Regiments, in their own words, 17–19 March

Everything the reconstruction has said about the two encircled regiments has come from above them — the corps report, the Front journal, the divisional diary. Their own papers say something more precise and less tidy, and they change the shape of what the 96th was sent to do.

The break-in, 17 March

The 90th went first. Its consolidated combat report № 101, written at midnight on 19 March, gives the whole thing: jump-off at 07.30 north and north-east of the wood south of Počas; the assault company takes Počas by noon; at 13.00, after the artillery preparation, the regiment breaks the German front edge at height 90.0 and drives north-east. By six that evening it had taken, in this order —

"Почас, Дзирнеки, Дудас, Арес, Трушли, Силини, Малли, Крумини, Лекуты, Калнини, Янайши"

— with its 1st battalion on the forest edge north and north-east of Jāņaiši and its 2nd on the Klaviņi–Jāņaiši road. The 90th took Jāņaiši on the evening of 17 March. Then it was stopped by small-arms fire, and — the phrase is the hinge of the whole episode — "пропустив через свои боевые порядки 87 гв.сп": it passed the 87th through its own battle formations.

The 87th's war diary describes the same hours from the other side of that hand-off. Its commander since 9 March was Guards Lt.Col. I. M. Tretyak, straight out of hospital from his third severe wound — the man a divisional patrol would be sent to find, by name, six days later. On the 15th the regiment had trained with tanks; on the 17th it used them:

"В 17.00 полк выступил, 1сб на танках ИС… В 21.00 Командир полка решил таранным ударом прорвать оборону пр-ка и 1сб на танках врезался в глубину обороны пр-ка. Уничтожив на своём пути до десяти орудий, полк вышел на рубеж леса — сев. опушка леса южнее Гребутниеки — заняв круговую оборону. Разбита пекарня пр-ка и взято две повозки хлеба. Захвачено 12 лошадей и уничтожено до 100 немцев."

Riflemen riding on the IS-122s of the 3rd Guards Heavy Tank Regiment, a battering-ram attack at nine at night, ten guns crushed on the way through, and then all-round defence in the wood south of Grebutnieki. They overran a German field bakery and took two cartloads of bread and twelve horses. Men who stop for bread expect to be there a while.

Two hundred metres

Then the sentence that revises the story:

"Пр-к, располагая достаточными оперативными и тактическими резервами, подтянул в р-он прорыва пехоту и до 20 самоходок, и ему удалось коридор прорыва уменьшить до 200 м. Весь день шла ожесточённая битва за расширение коридора, но успеха не добились."

The corridor was never completely severed. It was squeezed to two hundred metres by German infantry and up to twenty assault guns, and the whole of the following day was spent in a savage fight to widen it, which failed.

That is the frame the 1st Battalion of the 96th was inside. It was not attacking into a sealed ring to cut a new way in; it was attacking north at the neck of a two-hundred-metre corridor with two Guards regiments beyond it. The counterattack at 11.00 — sixty men, six tanks and assault guns out of Jāņaiši — was the German effort on that neck from the inside. It did not close it. And it explains the corps' choice of words, «для восстановления положения», restoring the situation, rather than anything about breaking through.

Coming out

The 90th's report continues: at 22.00 on the 17th it followed the 87th into the breach with two battalions and the regimental gun battery, moving by Kalniņi and the forest ride north-west of Jāņaiši; by 05.00 on the 18th it was at the copse south of Kuliēni, met heavy machine-gun fire from the heights west of Grebutnieki, fell back into the wood 500 m south-east of Dovas and defended facing west, north-west and south-west. Then:

"В 20.00 18.03.45г. полк согласно устного приказания по радио выступил из занимаемого района, оставив 1 с.б. для прикрытия… и к 4.00 19.03.45 прорвав передний край обороны пр-ка в районе 300 м. зап. Янайши сосредоточился Калнини."

The exit was ordered by radio, not fought for on the regiments' own initiative — the 87th's diary uses the same construction, «1сб получил приказ выйти из тыла пр-ка» — and it came back out through the German line three hundred metres west of Jāņaiši at four in the morning, a covering battalion last.

What it cost, and what it brought: "За время боёв 17, 18 и 19.03.45г. полк потерял убитыми и ранеными 175 чел., 7 лошадей, 1 45мм орудие." Against eleven guns, thirteen machine guns, about a hundred and fifty rifles and submachine guns, three lorries, two tractors, a food dump, four horses, five loaded carts, three telephone sets, and up to fifty prisoners.

One caution on dates. The 87th's diary runs a day ahead of the divisional records here — its entry headed «16 марта – 17 марта» carries the 14.00 artillery preparation and the 17.00 advance that the higher records place on 17 March, and it dates the withdrawal to the 18th against the division's night of the 19th. The 90th's combat reports, written the same day and timed to the hour, are the better authority for the calendar; the diary is the better authority for what it felt like.

ЦАМО ф. 6370, оп. 200593, д. 1 — журнал боевых действий 87-го гв. сп, лл. 56 об.–58 · ЦАМО ф. 6379, оп. 210850с, д. 10 — боевые донесения 90-го гв. сп, лл. 115–117

The other pocket

8th Guards (Panfilov) Rifle Division, 18–28 March

The 19th and 30th Guards Rifle Regiments of the Panfilov Division were cut off in the Danči area the same night as the 87th and 90th here, in the neighbouring corps. Their ordeal ran ten days longer.

By 25 March the Germans were squeezing the ring with elements of three divisions and calling on the encircled men to surrender over loudspeakers. Supply came in on men's backs along forest tracks at night — a little ammunition, dry bread, sugar, tinned food. Most soldiers carried two submachine guns, one Soviet and one captured.

On 28 March the 67th Rifle Regiment of the 22nd Guards Rifle Division, offered for the purpose by the commander of the 19th Guards Rifle Corps, attacked with an attached company and the fire of several artillery battalions, took a series of German abatis and blockhouses, and opened a gate two to three kilometres wide.

The Panfilov men came out through it without losing a single man, carrying more than a hundred wounded with them — among them their regimental commander, Ivan Leontyevich Shapshayev, who had lost an arm and was later made a Hero of the Soviet Union.

It is worth setting that beside what happened on this ground, three kilometres to the east, where the wounded of the 96th were still being carried in from the forward edge on the fourth and fifth day.

The armour that was with them

3rd Guards Heavy Tank Regiment and 1048th SP Artillery Regiment, 18–27 March

The war diary of the armoured and mechanised troops staff of the 10th Guards Army — a separate directorate, keeping its own journal one paragraph per unit per day — puts tanks alongside the 1st Battalion on 18 March, which no infantry document does. The 3rd Guards Separate Heavy Tank Regiment, IS-122s, was split between the two halves of the crisis: its 1st and 2nd companies went in with the 87th Guards Rifle Regiment and were caught in the pocket with it; its 3rd and 4th companies fought all day with the 96th.

"3 и 4 тк. роты во взаимодействии 96/30 гв. СД вели бой с атакующей пехотой и танками пр-ка из направления: Янайши, Дакас. За день отбито шесть контратак пр-ка. В 16.00 18.3.45 г. 3 и 4 т. роты во взаимодействии с 96/30 сд атаковали пр-ка в направлении Янайши, атака успеха не имела."

Six counterattacks, not one. The 11.00 attack that cost the battalion commander his leg was the first of six that day, all of them out of Jāņaiši and Dakas, and at 16.00 what was left of the regiment attacked once more toward Jāņaiši with the tanks and got nowhere. The tank regiment's own cost that day was three men killed and five officers and NCOs wounded.

The same entry, for the following day, is the only line in any of these files that states the encirclement as a fact rather than describing its effects: "В период вывода танков 1-й и 2-й Т. роты из окружения, один танк застрял в болоте." During the withdrawal of the 1st and 2nd companies' tanks from encirclement, one tank stuck in the bog. That is the 87th's pocket, reported by a third headquarters that had no reason to editorialise.

The 1048th Self-Propelled Artillery Regiment — SU-100s, twenty of them and one SU-85, 231 men — has left the closest thing to a first-hand account of this ground. It came under the 15th Guards Rifle Corps on the evening of 18 March expressly to support the 96th, marching Pampāļi–Cepļi–Ozoli–Čubas–Zaļmuguri–Počas–Gludas, and took fire positions on the unnamed heights east of Kalniņi with orders to beat off tank counterattacks from the direction of Eglеs.

At noon on 19 March, after the artillery preparation, it attacked toward Eglеs with the 96th's infantry and took Jāņaiši by 18.00. Its losses that day: one SU-100 burned, two knocked out, one man killed, ten wounded — and by name, the regiment's chief of staff Guards Major Damadayev A. M. and six junior lieutenants: Kuznetsov, Anichkin, Voronchuk, Toroshchin, Nikishin, Borodin.

It stayed on the ground until April, and it names the enemy repeatedly and consistently: "Части 12 ТД противника упорно обороняются в лесу сев. Эглес. На опушках леса имеются в наличии закопанные тяжелые танки и самоходные орудия" — 12. Panzer-Division, holding the wood north of Eglеs with heavy tanks and assault guns dug in along the wood edges. In early April 12. Panzer was relieved there by 11. Infanterie-Division and 329. Infanterie-Division.

It also carries the only prisoner statement in the whole run. On 25 March a German came over: a newly arrived regiment was in the sector, of one battalion in three companies of a hundred and fifty men each, and its number could not be established.

The Panfilov pocket has an armour footnote too, and it settles the date. On the night of 27/28 March the 957th SP Artillery Regiment was given the task of reaching the ride 700 m west of Dzintari "и тем расчистить путь для выхода окружённых подразделений 8 СД" — to clear the path for the encircled sub-units of the 8th to come out — and reported the task in the main accomplished after a hard night action; two T-34s of the 34th Guards Tank Brigade worked at breaking the ring from 11.00 on the 28th. That is a second, separate encirclement ten days after Dakas, and it should not be confused with the one on this ground.

ЦАМО ф. 354, оп. 5818, д. 113 — журнал боевых действий БТ и МВ 10 гв. А, лл. 30–42 · ЦАМО ф. 4387, оп. 170876с, д. 1 — история 1048-го самоходного артиллерийского полка, лл. 128–134

From the other side

Heeresgruppe Kurland daily situation maps, 16–22 March 1945

Everything below comes from one series. The German army general staff's operations branch — Gen.St.d.H., Op.Abt. IIIb — kept a daily situation map of Heeresgruppe Kurland, drawn on the printed Europa 1:300 000 sheet and marked Geheime Kommandosache · Chef-Sache · nur durch Offizier. Each is timed abends: the position as the staff understood it at the end of that day. The sheets were captured and taken to Podolsk, where they sit as fond 500, findbuch 12459, digitised and free to read. Seven consecutive evenings survive across this battle, from its eve to its sixth day, each carrying a subordination chart, an armour strength table, and from 21 March a casualty and weather line.

0Divisions of the 10th Guards Army plotted on the German map on the evening of 16 March
75Soviet tanks claimed destroyed by 16. Armee on 18 March, against nine the day before
49 → 29Running Panzer IV lang in 12. Panzer-Division, 15 to 20 March
6.The battle was renamed the Sixth Battle of Courland on 18 March

They did not see it coming

On the sheet for the evening of 16 March the 10th Guards Army is not on the map. The red overprint in front of XXXVIII. Panzerkorps carries divisional numbers and corps designations, but the army itself is not identified and neither is the corps that would attack the next afternoon.

By the evening of the 17th they had it. Far to the south-west, in the blank margin of the sheet over Samogitia, a boxed red annotation reads 10. Gd. Armee with its corps — VII., XV. and XIX. Guards Rifle — and its divisions: 8, 22, 29, 30, 56, 65, 85 and 119 Guards Rifle. The 30th is his. The same box reappears on the sheets that follow, and from the 19th and 20th the corps designations are also plotted forward, in the line.

So the surprise is narrower than it first looks, and more exact. On the eve the army is nowhere on the sheet. By the evening of the day it attacked, the German intelligence staff had named it, its three corps and its eight divisions. What they had not done on the 16th was expect it — and what they never did, on any sheet, was place that army in front of XXXVIII. Panzerkorps before it arrived there.

One caution on the geography of that box. It sits over Lithuania, a hundred kilometres behind the front, which is where a staff writes an identification it holds but has not yet fixed to a sector — not where it believes the army to be. The same corner of the sheet carries a large red ring round Alsėdžiai enclosing 28 SD, 4 Pz.Br, 5 Pz.Rgt and 10 St.G.Rgt, and the boundary line of the 2nd Baltic Front. Whether the 10. Gd. Armee box is also on the 16 March sheet in that same corner has not been checked — the eve crops we read covered the Frauenburg rectangle only.

The reserve went in

Heeresgruppe Kurland held two mobile divisions back from the line: 14. Panzer and 12. Panzer, the latter listed split as Ma. 12. Pz. and Tle. 12. Pz. — the bulk and the elements.

On the evening of 17 March, with the breach already open, 12. Panzer was still in army group reserve. On the evening of the 18th it stands in the line under XXXVIII. Panzerkorps, and the reserve is down to 14. Panzer alone.

The six tanks that came out of Jāņaiši at 11.00 on 18 March against 1st Battalion belonged to a division that had been the theatre's last uncommitted armour twenty-four hours earlier.

And it was already standing there. On the eve sheet the map shows 12. Pz. (o. 1 Brig.) circled just west of Frauenburg, by Pumpuri and Butāni — a few kilometres behind the ground it would counterattack across. Its detached brigade is circled separately at Durbe, eighty kilometres west, with 14. Panzer. The force table registers the split in its own way, giving 18. Armee 1½ mobile divisions and 16. Armee ½. So "army group reserve" on 17 March did not mean somewhere in the rear: it meant parked behind Frauenburg, waiting.

The battle changed its name

The 17 March sheet labels the fighting 2. Phase – 5. Kurlandschlacht — the second phase of the fifth battle, running from 3 March.

The 18 March sheet is headed 6. Kurlandschlacht, and counts 17 March as the first day of attack. Every sheet after it does the same.

The Sixth Battle of Courland acquired its name on the day Guards Major Yermak was hit. The staff renamed it because the two days that had just passed no longer fitted inside the battle they had been fighting.

XXXVIII. Panzerkorps, evening by evening

The corps that held this ground on the morning of 17 March was a security-battalion kampfgruppe, a worn infantry division and one more division. Within forty-eight hours it had an infantry division and the theatre armoured reserve added to it. Kgr. 122 — the remnant of the 122nd Infantry Division — consisted of one regiment of the 81st, security battalions 507 and 989, and a machine-gun battalion.

The army boundary swung across the 11th

On 16 March the 11. Infanterie-Division belonged to II. Korps of 18. Armee. On the 17th it appears under XXXVIII. Panzerkorps of 16. Armee. On the 20th it is back with 18. Armee, under L. Korps.

Look at where it is drawn across those five sheets and it barely moves. The division stayed on the ground at Dakas; the army boundary swung over it and back, putting the whole threatened sector under one army for exactly as long as the crisis lasted.

By 22 March the 11th is being propped up with battalions borrowed from the 263rd, the 122nd and the 563rd Volksgrenadier — three lenders for one division.

A practical consequence for anyone searching German files: for 17–19 March look under AOK 16; for the 16th and from the 20th, under AOK 18.

A named position

Running east and west south of Frauenburg, the sheets carry a blue line labelled Striķi-Riegel — a switch position named for the village of Striķi.

A Riegel with a name existed on paper before the attack rather than being improvised under it. Set that beside the divisional record for 18 March, which says the main attack at 10.00 went in against armoured pillboxes. Armoured pillboxes belong to a prepared system, and this is the system they belonged to.

The division came apart

By 22 March 12. Panzer is no longer one formation. The subordination chart puts Ma. 12. Pz., annotated with the number 25, under XXXVIII. Panzerkorps, and a second brigade numbered 5 under VI. SS-Korps to the north-east. The map marks the group at Lekusi 12. Pz. (o. 1 Brig.) — without one brigade.

The two numbers match the division's two Panzergrenadier regiments. Regiment 25 is the one the Soviet documents name as taking the tree line Jāņaiši–Purviņi on the morning of 18 March, and Regiment 25's battlegroup is the half that stayed on this ground.

What the week cost 12. Panzer-Division
