The tables lag the map: each sheet carries the most recent divisional return rather than the day's, so the strength as at 20 March appears only on the sheet of 22 March. Twenty running Panzer IV lang gone in five days, against four vehicles struck off the books outright — so most of the loss is damage and mechanical failure rather than destruction, which is what a week of committed fighting does to a panzer division. It is also a figure that exists nowhere in the Soviet records, because nobody on this side could count it.

Total claimed211 · 18. Armee 19written under the columns by the staff on the sheet of 29 March

The tank-claim column is 16. Armee's. The 18. Armee column on the same table is nearly empty — a single 8 for 17 and 18 March, dashes either side, then 6 on 21 March and nothing after — which is the measure of how completely this was 16. Armee's battle. Whether that 8 belongs to the 18th alone is not settled: the sheets of 23 and 25 March brace the two dates together against it, while the sheet of 24 March shows a dash for the 17th and the 8 against the 18th. The figures themselves are also revised as returns come in — 23 March stands at 13 on two sheets and 18 on the third, 24 March at 4 then 5 — so these are running claims, not a closed ledger. Tank claims are claims and run high; what they establish is shape, not quantity. Eighteen March stands at eight times the previous day and nearly three times the next — the day the armoured fighting peaked, and the day 1st Battalion was broken. The casualty lines give own losses against an assessed enemy figure, and they lag. The lag is not fixed: the sheet of 17 March reports 16 March at 129 men and 540, and the sheet of 18 March reports the same day again at 260 and 5,649, both marked Teilmeldung — a partial return, repeated and revised upward when the next day's figures had not yet come in. So 17 March has no return at all in the sheets read, and every date on these lines has to be read off the sheet rather than assumed. 23 March is the heaviest day in the series at 1,650 men. 18 March stands at 1,132 — but that figure explicitly excludes VI. SS Corps, and is a partial return where the 23 March figure is marked as including late reports, so the two are not comparable and the true total for the 18th is unknown. Set it against the 10th Guards Army's 2,302 for the same day. It is also the only day on which the German staff booked more of its own men lost than it credited to the enemy — 1,132 against 514, more than two to one. On every other day the ratio runs the other way: 129 against 540, 260 against 5,649, 792 against 6,224, 1,254 against 3,735, 653 against 5,294. Both halves of the 18 March line are read at high magnification and both are as given.

The sheet of 26 March adds the only cumulative figure in the run, written across the panel in its own hand: "Die Verluste b. 16. Armee seit 1. März haben die Zahl 12 000 überschritten" — the losses of 16. Armee since 1 March have passed twelve thousand. That is one army, the one holding Saldus, in twenty-six days. The eve sheet gives the other end of that arithmetic: "Eigene Verluste bei 16. Armee v. 1.3.–7.3.: 2500 Mann" — two and a half thousand in the first week. So something over nine thousand of the twelve fell in the nineteen days that followed, and the two heaviest single days in the run are 18 and 23 March. The same line is repeated on the sheet of the 27th.

And on 27 March the claim column shows a dash against both armies for the first time since the battle opened. The armoured fighting had stopped, and it never restarted: 18. Armee claimed five on the 28th and then nothing, and on the sheet of 29 March the staff ruled a line under each column and wrote the totals — 19 for 18. Armee, 211 for 16. Armee. Set the second figure beside the eve sheet’s note of 205 claimed in the first ten days of March, and the Sixth Battle cost 16. Armee’s gunners about as many claimed tanks as the whole earlier phase of the month. The closing sheets also settle the date the battle began. Four of them carry an Angriffstag count — 28.3 the thirteenth, 29.3 the fourteenth, 1.4 the seventeenth, 2.4 the eighteenth — and every one of the four back-counts to 16 March 1945 as the first day. That is the German staff’s own answer to a question this reconstruction has had to leave open, and it agrees with Mangulis against the 18 March date used by most of the literature. The weather matters for a reason particular to this reconstruction: 18 March broke clear and hard-frozen, and by the 21st it was above zero in storm and sleet, with the sheets noting that the coastal ice would no longer bear. Wounded were still being carried in from the forward edge on the 22nd, 23rd and 24th. Whoever lay out on that ground lay through the thaw.

What this series can and cannot show

At 1:300 000 a kilometre is three millimetres. Eglеs, Jāņaiši and Purviņi are not on these sheets; Dakas and Striķi are, and they bracket the ground. The series draws divisional frontages and boundaries at the end of the day, so neither the encirclement of the 87th and 90th at Dakas nor the Panfilov regiments' pocket appears on it — both were sealed off overnight, and by nightfall the line was closed. That is not a distortion. It is an accurate record of where the front stood at dusk, and from the German side an infiltration that was contained was a success rather than a crisis. The event exists in their papers as a sentence in a daily report, not as a mark on an OKH map. Corps-level maps at 1:100 000, in findbuch 12474 and 12475, are the level at which local penetrations were drawn.

TsAMO fond 500, findbuch 12459 · digitised at wwii.germandocsinrussia.org

What the Soviet gunners had plotted, 13–16 March

There is one more German order of battle for this ground, and it is not German. It is what the Soviet artillery staff believed it was shooting at, written down three days before the attack. It survives in the incoming-documents file of the 63rd Guards Artillery Regiment — the divisional artillery regiment of the 30th Guards — and it is worth setting beside the Lagekarten, because the two disagree in an instructive way.

The reconnaissance instruction of the artillery group, timed 20.00 on 13 March, opens:

"Противник силами 11 полевого запасного батальона 11 ПД, 2/503 ПП, 1/501 ПП, 290 ПД обороняется на рубеже: КАУПИ–ОЗОЛЫ выс. 90,0–ПОЧАС СПРИГУЛИ РУПКИ выс. 92,0. Ближайшим тактическим резервом является 290 полевой запасной батальон 290 ПД…"

The enemy in front of the break-in sector was read as the field replacement battalion of 11. Infanterie-Division and two battalions of 290. Infanterie-Division — II./Gren.Rgt. 503 and I./Gren.Rgt. 501 — with 290. Infanterie-Division's own field replacement battalion as the nearest tactical reserve, in the wood north-east of Saukulis. 290. Infanterie-Division does not appear anywhere else in this reconstruction. It is not on the Lagekarten sheets for these days and it is not in any Soviet document read so far; it enters only here, in the gunners' target intelligence, and it belongs in the picture with that qualification attached.

The same instruction plots the German guns by farm, which no other document does:

"Артиллерия противника группируется в районах: 75 и 105 мм калибр ЯНАЙШИ, ДАМБИЙ, ЛОКУТИ; 150 мм калибра — ДИДЖАРИ ШПАУКИ. Миномёты пр-ка располагаются в районах: ЯУНБЕЛТЕС, ПЛОШЕНИЭКИ, ДЕРИ, МАЗКАЛНИ."

Seventy-fives and hundred-and-fives at Jāņaiši, Dambji and Lokuti; one-fifties at Didžari and Špauki; mortars at Jaunbeltes, Ploceņieki, Deri and Mazkalni. The attack order of 22.00 on 16 March refines it further: one 150 mm battery at Kaupiņi, three 105 mm batteries at Bites, Mazenieki and Jāņaiši, two 75 mm at Čalli and Ploceņieki, three 81.4 mm mortar batteries 200 m south-west of Rubeņi and at Dzirnieki and Gludas.

And the description of the position itself, from the same sheet: "прерывчатая траншея полного профиля… блиндажи-укрытия в два-три наката. На отдельных участках имеется проволока-спираль «Бруно», минные поля и лесные завалы." Intermittent full-profile trench, dugouts under two and three layers of logs, concertina wire, minefields and forest abatis — which is the same position the 96th's own documents describe from the front, four days later.

ЦАМО ф. 10735, оп. 1, д. 4 — входящие документы 63-го гв. артиллерийского полка, лл. 172, 192

The men on the other side

The Lagekarten draw formations, not people. The army group's own appointment list of 20 April 1945 supplies the names, and where its seit dates fall in April they record a formal appointment rather than an arrival, so the March post-holder usually has to be recovered elsewhere. What follows is the chain of command above the ground west-south-west of Frauenburg during the ten days.

The 16th Army changed hands on the eve of the battle. General der Infanterie Ernst-Anton von Krosigk took AOK 16 on 10 March and was killed in action on 16 March 1945 near Kandava, the day before the first Angriffstag. General der Gebirgstruppe Friedrich-Jobst Volckamer von Kirchensittenbach took it over at once and held it until the capitulation — while continuing to command L. Armeekorps, which he did not give up until 12 April. So the army holding Saldus fought the Sixth Battle under a man who had inherited it the previous day and was running a corps at the same time. Above him, Heeresgruppe Kurland was commanded not by Hilpert but by Generaloberst Dr. Lothar Rendulic, 10–24 March; Hilpert only from the 25th.

Two seit dates fall inside the run-up and are worth the note: 329. Infantry Division changed its operations officer on 15 March, and 14. Panzer changed its commander the same day. Neither division was newly arrived; both changed the man who would run the coming week.

The regiment that held Eglеs

Hauptmann Werner Buxa, commander of the I. Bataillon. He survived, wrote the division's history in 1952, and died in 1998.

Award citations are the one class of German document for this week that survives and is readable. The recommendation for Oberst Löbe's Oak Leaves, granted on 29 April 1945, recites four actions, and the fourth is 16–18 March 1945. It names the line his regiment was taking over: Balosi / Jegles – Dambji – Maeenieki.

Those are Baloži, Eglеs, Damji and Mazenieki. The Soviet corps report for the same days has the 96th Guards Rifle Regiment digging in в районе ЭГЛЕС and the 93rd attacking на южн. опушке леса сев. ДАМЬИИ и МАЗЕНИЭКИ before holding the line ПУРВИНИ, МАЗЕНИЭКИ. Both sides name the same farms for the same days. It is the first point in this reconstruction where a German document and a Soviet document can be laid on the same square of ground.

So the formation opposite the 1st Battalion was Grenadier-Regiment 44 "Ostpreußen" of the 11th Infantry Division, and the battalion whose sector gave way was its I. Bataillon under Hauptmann Werner Buxa.

The citation's account of those days: the Soviets attacked at 11.00 with overwhelming superiority, which it puts at two Guards divisions; Löbe kept contact with his battalions through close-quarter fighting at the regimental command post; at 01.45 on 18 March enemy tanks broke through the I. Bataillon sector, laying both flanks open; he took twenty men against the enemy who had got into his rear, then brought up Sturmgeschütze to close the penetration, and the citation claims over a hundred Soviet dead.

A caution on award dates, which are not action dates. Buxa's Knight's Cross of 23 March is for 15 February, when he rode an assault gun through to the encircled defenders of Höhe 103.5. Engelien's Oak Leaves of 16 March are retrospective, for the Third Battle of Courland and a second counterattack at the end of January. Neither decoration was earned in the week reconstructed here, and both would mislead if read as if it were.

Vorschlag for the Eichenlaub, Oberst Heinz-Oskar Löbe (site spelling "Laebe"), tracesofwar.com/persons/36037 · 15 гв.ск, отчёт о боевых действиях, л. 18

Both battalions, and the men who were decorated for this ground

Grenadier-Regiment 44 had only two infantry battalions by 1945, the second formed out of the old third. Both commanders were decorated for these three days, and between them the citations account for the whole of the regiment's infantry.

Hauptmann Heinz-Georg Ritter commanded the II. Bataillon. His Knight's Cross, granted on 20 April 1945, is for an action of 17 March 1945 "near Jegles" — Eglеs, on the day the offensive opened. The recommendation has him and his staff going forward and occupying part of the front line themselves, fighting "during the entire day… from his foxhole with Panzerfaust and Sturmgewehr in hand", and after repeated Soviet penetrations personally leading "his ever dwindling number of men in a counterthrust" to restore the line. He was born in Danzig in 1917 and died in Schleswig-Holstein in 2010, aged ninety-two.

Alongside them, the divisional artillery. Stabsgefreiter Arno Wienrich, a forward observer of the 2nd Battery of Artillery Regiment 11, was decorated for the same battle, dated in his citation to 18–31 March: when the Soviets encircled a German strongpoint near Frauenburg he brought the divisional guns down on the attack until it broke off, was wounded, and went on directing fire "for another 12 hours under severe pain until a replacement finally arrived".

And the divisional commander's own citation names the ground. Generalleutnant Feyerabend received the Knight's Cross on 5 April 1945 for the Sixth Battle: "Fighting between Lekutis and Dudas, the Division absorbed the attacking power of the Soviet 10th Guards Army with commendable steadfastness." Lekuti and Dudas are farms on the same 1:75,000 sheet as Jāņaiši, and Dudas appears in the Soviet burial records for 17–20 March.

Four citations — Löbe, Ritter, Wienrich, Feyerabend — converge on the same farms in the same week. They survive because award recommendations are the one class of German document from this month that was filed away from the front, and they are indexed by name rather than by place. Every German order, daily report and war diary for this sector in March 1945 is gone.

tracesofwar.com, translated Vorschläge: Ritter persons/30115, Wienrich persons/36045, Feyerabend persons/4322

Where they are buried

The German dead of this ground lie at Strazdi in Novadnieki parish, 56°36'35" N / 22°27'25" E, a few kilometres south-west of Saldus — the largest German collective cemetery in the Baltic states, holding some 23,700 men with room for thirty thousand, opened in 1999 and still receiving reburials. The older cemetery inside Saldus town, with about two thousand graves, was dissolved and moved here from 1994. Only a small proportion of the names has ever been published; the visitors' centre keeps the books of names, boards on the six Kurland battles, and a cabinet of things relatives left at the crosses, "darunter sind viele Fotos der Gefallenen".

A 389-name list compiled from German civil death registers gives place of death and, sometimes, unit — information the official database does not carry. It is a sample, weighted heavily to men from Brandenburg and Saxony-Anhalt, so absence from it means nothing. Six of its entries fall inside the ten days, and two are named to the town: Gefreiter Franz Stolpmann, born 2 September 1924, killed 18 March 1945 bei Frauenburg, and Obergefreiter Hans Joachim Bahr, born 11 August 1921, killed 21 March 1945 bei Frauenburg. Neither carries a unit. A week earlier, on 11 March, Oberschütze Erwin Beling died in Osolini, südw. Frauenburg — Ozoliņi, one of the farms the Soviet corps report names on the 18–19 March line.

The same list confirms four more of the farm names in this reconstruction as places where Germans were killed: Purviņi three times over, Baloži twice, Laugaļi and Dadži.

Kriegsgräberstätte Saldus, Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge · name list transcribed 1.7.2025 by R. Krukenberg, denkmalprojekt.org

A German account of 19 March, and why it is not from this ground

The German veterans' site kurland-kessel.de carries twenty-one personal accounts, and one of them is dated to the right day. Leutnant Willi Krück commanded a company of schwere Heeres-Panzerjäger-Abteilung 667 — an anti-tank battalion that gave up its 8.8 cm guns in January 1945, was renamed Panzergrenadier-Brigade Kurland and carried on as infantry. His orders for 19 March 1945 were to push forward with two platoons into a Soviet assembly area after an artillery strike at 08.00.

It reads at first like the mirror image of this reconstruction. A trench empty to the left as far as a railway embankment and no contact to the right; an abandoned German machine gun and its ammunition found in the position; a runner sent back to the command post who never returned; shelled woodland in front, full of tall stumps, giving the attackers cover; and at dusk the survivors gathered on a clearing between the trench and the railway line. Krück places it südlich von Frauenburg.

The map does not allow it. The Jelgava–Liepāja line is the only broad-gauge railway in the sector and the only track an armoured train could run on. On the Latvian 1:75 000 sheet it passes through Ciecere some eleven to twelve kilometres due north of Jāņaiši. Dakas is four kilometres north of the farm and still eight short of the rails, with the Striķi position and the German rear area in between. On the OKH sheets the front runs parallel to the line and south of it along the whole southern face of the pocket, and closes on it only far to the east-north-east, beyond Blīdene. Krück was some twenty-five kilometres away, on the other side of Saldus. He hedged it himself, in a phrase easy to read past: the ground was the battlefield im weitesten Sinne — in the broadest sense.

What he is worth is not the ground but the troops holding it. His men, he writes, "kannten den infanteristischen Angriff nur als Übung während der Rekrutenzeit" — knew the infantry attack only as an exercise from their recruit training. They were East Prussian anti-tank gunners who had spent the winter hearing what was happening at home. Eighty were to have attacked that morning. The Soviet preparation opened an hour early and in a neighbouring sector, so the attack was cancelled and the two platoons went over to the defence in the abandoned trench they had just occupied. Twenty-seven gathered at dusk. Then the armoured train came up in the half-light, stopped level with them, opened fire with everything it had and laid it short, and seven walked back. That is what the German infantry opposite the 15th Guards Rifle Corps was made of by the third day of the battle, and it belongs beside the divisional numbers on the maps. Krück also dates the offensive to 18 March — a third voice for that reading, against the sheets that count from the 17th.

Willi Krück, Erlebnisbericht 10, kurland-kessel.de · geometry measured on Latvian 1:75 000 sheet 19-Saldus, 1929, and the Lage Ost sheet of 1.3.1945

The sky

who the aircraft at 12.45 belonged to

The regiment's report of 18 March contains one line about aircraft — «В 12.45 отмечались пролёты самолётов». No number, no type, no markings, no direction. It is the only mention of aircraft in any document on this ground and it does not say whose they were. What follows is an attempt to answer that from the order of battle, and it ends in a probability rather than a fact.

What the Luftwaffe still had

Luftflotte 1 was the German air command in Courland. The last strength return available is 10 January 1945: 244 aircraft, 214 of them serviceable — and taking out the Ju 52s of I./TG 1, about 199 combat aircraft, 172 serviceable, for the whole bridgehead. No March return has been found and this reconstruction does not invent one.

By 18 March that figure had certainly fallen. Nachtschlachtgruppe 3, the only night ground-attack Gruppe in Kurland, was disbanded on 13 March — five days before. NAGr 5 and the Stab of JG 54 were dissolved in the same month. And the January return itself records the constraint that mattered more than airframes: for want of fuel the aircraft had to stay on the ground most of the time.

And where it had to fly from

Both airfields on this axis had been given up months earlier, and both are named on German charts in their German forms. Frauenburg — Saldus itself — held III./SG 3 and NAGr 5 from October to December 1944; both moved out, SG 3 to Zabeln and NAGr 5 to Cīrava. Schrunden — Skrunda held the Stab of JG 54 over the same months; it also went to Cīrava.

From March 1945 the nearest German field still flying was Zabeln (Sabile), about 43 km north, where III./SG 3 remained to the end of the war. Everything else — Cīrava, Grobiņa, Liepāja, Ventspils — lies 65 to 98 km off. An earlier note in this project put the nearest field at forty-three kilometres; that was wrong by Zabeln, and the figure is corrected here.

What the Red Army had just been given

The 15th Air Army supported this front, and in the weeks before this attack it was reinforced out of the 3rd Air Army as the neighbouring front's sector was wound up: the 5th Guards Bomber Aviation Corps and the 7th Assault Aviation Corps from 1 February 1945, and the 1st Guards Fighter Aviation Corps from 3 March 1945 — fifteen days before this morning.

A second correction to this project's own notes: those three corps had been recorded here as arriving together on 1–3 March. Two of the three came a month earlier. The transfer is real; the compressed date was not.

And 18 March was not an ordinary day in the sector. It is the opening day of the Sixth Courland Battle, whose axis was Saldus toward Liepāja — precisely this ground.

So: at a quarter to one on the opening day of an offensive, over an attacking Soviet army that had just been handed three air corps, with no German flying unit inside forty kilometres and the only night ground-attack group disbanded the week before — the aircraft were almost certainly Soviet, most plausibly Il-2s working the sector. That is a judgement from the order of battle and not a reading of any document. III./SG 3 at Zabeln was still flying and could in principle have been overhead. The one thing that would settle it is the 15th Air Army's own operational report for 18 March 1945, which has not been read. One line has since been added to the other side of the scale. The 10th Guards Army's own commander records that in the run-up to this attack the weather was «unfavourable to the actions of aviation» as well as to artillery — morning fog, snow melting by day. He is describing the preparatory period rather than 18 March itself, and it does not decide the question, but it belongs here.

The enemy nobody can read

290. Infanterie-Division, and the hole where its records should be

On 18 March the Soviet divisional artillery staff plotted the formation facing this ground as 290. Infanterie-Division. The identification holds. What does not exist is anything the division itself wrote.

Who was opposite

The division was in Courland, and its commander from 18 August 1944 to 25 April 1945 was Generalmajor Hans-Joachim Baurmeister — «Am 18. August 1944 mit der Führung der 290. Infanterie-Division beauftragt». Generalmajor from 9 November 1944 and never promoted beyond it. He was succeeded on 25 April 1945, went into Soviet captivity with the rest of Kurland, and died there on 22 February 1950.

A working note in this project had him as a Generalleutnant. He was not.

A regiment that should not have existed

The reference works record Grenadier-Regiment 503 as gone: «Das Regiment wurde im Dezember 1944 aufgelöst, die Reste kamen zum Grenadier-Regiment 501». The award record says otherwise. On 14 February 1945 Anton Müller received the Oak Leaves to the Knight's Cross as Hauptmann und Kommandeur des II. Bataillons, Grenadier-Regiment 503, 290. Infanterie-Division — a command certified as existing two months after the regiment was supposedly dissolved.

He had had the Knight's Cross itself in September 1944 as Führer of I./Grenadier-Regiment 501, which was itself a reconstruction: the original I. Bataillon went in the winter of 1942/43 and the III. was renumbered as I. on 22 July 1944.

It is a small thing, and it is set down precisely because it is the kind of small thing that decides whether a formation one has confidently identified was actually there in the shape one imagines.

A claim withdrawn

An earlier working note in this project carried a Knight's Cross citation to Amsberg covering 17–28 March 1945 and naming the 8th and 47th as his opponents — which would have made him the German commander of the operation against the other pocket. The man is real and the division is right: Oberst i.G. Joachim von Amsberg, commanding Grenadier-Regiment 502 of the 290th, taken prisoner in Courland in May 1945.

The award is not. His nomination was rejected on 9 May 1945 because the intermediate commanders had not endorsed it, and the Knight's Cross was granted only by a ruling of the order commission in 1981. No text of the recommendation is published anywhere reachable, and nothing in any accessible source connects him to those dates or those formations. The claim is withdrawn and does not appear anywhere else in this reconstruction.

And the hole

There is no German counterpart to any of the Soviet paper here, and there cannot be from the obvious place. The Bundesarchiv holding for the division, RH 26-290, has a stated span of 1940 to 1944, and the deepest any of its sub-series reaches is the beginning of January 1944: the Ia war diary to early January 1944, the Ib to December 1943, the Ic to the end of December 1943, the IIa to May 1943. There is no 1945 in it at all.

Every German unit, position and gun drawn on the maps in this reconstruction is therefore drawn from what Soviet observers reported seeing. That is a real limit on everything blue in this document and it should be read as one.

Two routes remain untried: AOK 18's war diary, RH 20-18, which is orderable remotely, and the divisional veterans' association, Kameraden-Hilfswerk 290. ID e.V. in Delmenhorst, which is still active — together with the divisional history by von Bock, Polach and Greve of 1986.

What everyone else recorded

the published accounts, and what they leave out

Three published or transcribed sources cover this division, this army and this ground. None of them describes 18 March 1945. Read together, their silences are as informative as the documents.

The division's own history

V. Yu. Volkov's From Tula to the Courland Peninsula is a memoir written along the combat path of the 30th Guards Rifle Division. It is not a short book, and it is not vague about Courland.

The January 1945 fight for the hamlet Karkliņi gets pages, and the line "Karkliņi is remembered by everyone who fought on the Courland peninsula." February gets its own treatment.

Then March 1945 arrives, and this is all of it:

The spring operation towards Saldus did not develop either. At the end of March, on the front commander's orders, the 10th Guards Army went over to the defence.

Eglеs, Jāņaiši, Dakas, Cherkasov, the 1st Battalion of the 96th — none of them appear anywhere in the book. The division's own published history disposes of the week in which one of its regiments lost a battalion and had its commander removed in a single subordinate clause.

The man inside the pocket wrote a book

For eighteen months this project had him three kilometres away, commanding a battalion of the 93rd. That was wrong, and the correction changes what his memoir is.

Guards Lieutenant-Colonel Ivan Moiseyevich Tretyak took over the 87th Guards Rifle Regiment on 9 March 1945, straight out of hospital from his third severe wound — «прибыл из госпиталя и принял полк», in the regiment's own war diary. It was the 87th that went into the pocket at Dakas eight days later. He was made Hero of the Soviet Union on 24 March 1945 and ended as an Army General and Deputy Minister of Defence of the USSR.

So the only published memoir by anyone inside that encirclement is his — chapter 10 of «Храбрые сердца однополчан», free at militera.

He confirms the shape of it. He took the regiment from Major Boronin. He names the objective — «задача по расчленению и разгрому войск противника в районе Гребутниеке, Салдус». He names his companion in the breach: «С нашим 87-м полком в брешь… проскочили половина 90-го гвардейского полка под командованием подполковника П. Похалюка» — half of the 90th, under Pakholyuk, which is the second regiment of the pocket and its commander, confirmed from inside it. And he confirms the withdrawal: «По радио нам передали приказ: выводить группу», and «Нам подсказали по радио маршруты выхода».

Then he differs, in three ways that matter.

The corridor. The 87th's own war diary says the Germans squeezed it to 200 metres and that the fight to widen it failed. The memoir says they closed it: «Дыру, образовавшуюся в результате нашего прорыва, гитлеровцы надежно закрыли» — securely closed. No width appears anywhere in the book.

The cost. «Наши потери были незначительными» — our losses were insignificant. The 90th alone booked 175 killed and wounded for 17–19 March.

And the 96th is not in the book. Not the regiment, not the relief attack, not the battalion destroyed trying to reach him. Neither are the 94th or the 98th. Neither is any date in March — the chapter has «первые сутки» and «вторые, на третьи сутки» and not one calendar date in it. Neither is the word encirclement, which he never uses of his own regiment, nor the word corridor, nor Dakas, nor Jāņaiši, nor any of the farms.

He was got out. He did not know, or did not record, what it cost the regiment next door.

On the text. These passages were read through an automated fetch of militera.lib.ru rather than transcribed by hand from a copy, and the same passages were pulled twice by different routes and came back identical. That is good evidence and it is not a verified transcription. Anything quoted from the memoir on screen should be checked against chapter 10 by eye first.

What the memoir gives that no document does. A clear frosty night that betrayed them — «А ночь выдалась не в нашу пользу — ясная, зоревая», «Легкий мартовский мороз прихватил землю», «Каждый шаг был слышен». Fifteen to seventeen kilometres covered in the dark, fighting, in three columns. The regimental command post moved «то в танк, то в машину, то теперь вот в сани» — into a tank, into a vehicle, and now into a sledge. Their own artillery falling behind them because they had outrun the fire plan: «Залпы орудий и „катюш“… пришлись по пустому месту — далеко позади боевых порядков нашего полка» — the mirror image of the 96th's «в 50-60 мт от пехоты!» the next day. Everything in supply except salt. Then snow and murk at first light for the way back out.

And one detail that would carry a film on its own: they fought the raid with captured German weapons, on principle, to save their own — so that «эхо разносило окрест звуки выстрелов немецкого оружия, русского слышно не было». The echo carried the sound of German weapons firing. Russian was not to be heard.

Elsewhere in the same chapter, the reason the attack was made the way it was: the German defence built as belts every one and a half to two kilometres, self-propelled guns shuttling between them, each belt breakable only after a heavy artillery preparation "which was not always within the combat capabilities of the attackers."

And then, once the fighting round Saldus began:

The Stavka demanded that the command of the 2nd Baltic Front "decisively activate combat operations." The instruction was passed down the chain at once, from senior to junior. Some commanders saw fit to strengthen it on their own account.

— Well then, sitting it out, are we? Can you even hear the war down where you are? — came the sarcasm down the telephone from army headquarters.
— We can hear it and see it, — we answered. — The Germans are shoving at us right now. We're firing back from the dugout.

That is the middle of 18 March. The two ends are already in the documents: a regiment sent into a seam at 01.20 against armoured pillboxes, and Govorov cancelling the whole offensive at 11.00 because there were no shells in Front depots. Between them sits pressure from above, arriving as sarcasm on a telephone line.

Three men buried at the farm

Jāņaiši has a burial record of its own, filed under Novadnieku parish. Three men lie there, all of the 19th Assault Engineer-Sapper Brigade RGK and its 94th separate assault engineer-sapper battalion — a unit already on the attachment list for this operation.

Krasnoarmeets Ivchenko, Aleksandr Ivanovich, born 1925, killed 23 March 1945, north-west of the farm.
Serzhant Akstyn, Nikolai Mikhailovich, born 1915, and Efreitor Golubev, Konstantin Andreyevich, born 1926, both killed 19 March 1945 at the forest edge 200 m north of the farm.

Two assault engineers killed on the tree line north of Jāņaiši on 19 March — the morning after the tanks of 12. Panzer and Panzergrenadier-Regiment 25 took it, and the day after 1st Battalion was counterattacked out of the farm.

Their burial return cites square 7579 on a 1:50,000 sheet of 1940 edition. The handover acts cite square 7678 on the 1:25,000 and 1:100,000 series. These may be different grids and are not reconciled here.

The recommendation sheet for Guards Starshina P. V. Vasiltsov of the 31st separate Guards reconnaissance company of the 29th Guards records that on 23 March 1945 a group of five scouts under his command was set the task of passing into the enemy rear in the area of the farm Jāņaiši, finding the unit of Hero of the Soviet Union Tretyak, clarifying its situation, delivering an order and locating a rear reconnaissance group. On the night of 28 March, carrying out that task, the group was spotted and fired on by two machine guns; on his command the Germans were surrounded and their firing points destroyed, and the task was completed without loss. Order of the Red Star, divisional order № 024/н of 30 June 1945.

One correction to the family transcription published in the local newspaper: it compresses the two dates into one. The task is set on the 23rd; the contact happens on the night of the 28th.

So the reconnaissance company of the 29th Guards was sent to find a regiment of its own division — Tretyak's 87th — which had to be located behind the German line, five days after the fighting, and reached by hand with a written order. That is not a battalion in the line. It is a unit out of contact with its own division, which is the state the 87th and 90th were left in at Dakas.

Set those together and the shape of the record becomes clear. Men died on this farm on the 19th and the 23rd and their graves were registered by name. A reconnaissance patrol crossed it on the 23rd and its commander was decorated for it. A future Deputy Minister of Defence held a battalion three kilometres away and won the Gold Star that week. And the only published account of the division that owned this ground says the operation did not develop.

Readings from the sheets are marked in the text where a figure or a signature could not be resolved with confidence at the available magnification.

On the map base. Sheet 19-Saldus is a 1929 edition of an 1911 survey with partial 1927 revision, so farms created under the 1920s land reform are missing from it. Jāņaiši, Piles, Bezzobji, Baloži, Verpeles, Lekuti, Počas, Zaļmuguri, Dadži, Kurpnieki and Dekšnieki are printed on it and are fixed; Purviņi, Mazānieki, Āres, Malli, Dambiņi, Dzervītes, Aizupji, Vanagi and Zariņi are placed from the bearings in the documents and are shown with dashed rings. Eglеs and Kalniņi are no longer among them: the schema of the 98th Gds Rifle Regt for 22.03.45 draws both at 1:12,500 with the regimental command post on Kalniņi, and three independent bearings on Eglеs survive in the handover acts — a track and ride junction 500 m north-east, an unnamed height 200 m north-east, and a forest track 600 m north. The Soviet grid references in the documents are in the SK-42 system, northing first: Podnieki is square 6978, Dadži and the boundary height 90.0 are square 7278, and the limit of the last attack on 21 March is the forest path in square 7678. That reading is now confirmed against a gridded sheet: the schematic of the artillery group's combat order of 23 March carries its grid numbers printed in the margins, northings 75 to 78 and eastings 79 to 81, which puts Eglеs at about easting 78 and Jāņaiši at about 80.
